newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: INTERVIEW-Acindar hopes to hike production.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Acindar hopes to hike production.

text.p: Acindar, Argentina's main maker of long steel products, hopes to hike output about 20 percent in three years to accompany expected growth in the local economy, said Chairman of the Board Arturo Acevedo.
"Economists are projecting 6.9 percent growth in the building sector in 96/97, 10.4 percent in 97/98 and 8.2 percent in 98/99," he told Reuters in an interview.
"If those projections materialize, we hope to be able to raise production to 1.2 million tonnes from 1.05 million."

Acindar has about 60 percent of the domestic market in long steel products. The building sector accounts for 44 percent of its domestic sales, followed by manufacturers at 29 percent and agribusiness with 11 percent.
Acevedo said a $120 million restructuring plan launched in 1992 is now starting to bear fruit.

Last week, Acindar announced a net profit of $20 million in the first nine months of its fiscal year 1996/97 against a net loss of $30 million in the same period of the previous year. Revenue increased to $433 million from $420 million.

"This is the first reporting period when we are reaping fruit from those efforts," Acevedo said. "We still have some measures to implement. Savings made in this period will be increased in coming years. The company's results will improve over time."
Acindar's main goal is to reduce its equity/debt ratio from about a 60/40 percent to a more reasonable 70/30 percent, said Acevedo, member of the family that controls the company.
Part of that reduction may come from the obligatory conversion of outstanding bonds into shares, Acevedo said.

"The program envisages mandatory conversion in four years but it pays interest only in the first; then, as from October, it will cease paying interest and it could be supposed holders will convert them as they have nothing to win if they wait."
"From that moment $30 million in debt could turn into equity," Acevedo said, adding that if expected economic growth materialized, the company would keep reducing its debt.
About 62 percent of Acindar's shares have been floated.
Acevedo said the 1992 revamping plan included the adoption of a business-unit structure and a commercial policy with more emphasis on added value and service.
For instance, Acindar sells pre-welded tailor-made mesh for the building sector. "Clients get them just 24 hours before using them and save manpower costs," he said.
Acevedo dismissed reports of Acindar having to import raw material from Brazil in disadvantageous conditions vis a vis Brazilian companies.
He said the average price for billets charged by three major Brazilian steelmakers was $217 while a U.S. prime producer charges $215.80. Acindar's billet price is $214.
He added that abundant and cheap gas in Argentine allows Acindar to use a 70 percent direct reduced iron or "synthetic scrap" and 30 percent scrap mix.
"That results in a very important advantage that allows us access to markets as far away as Taiwan or Korea. We use as much gas as the city of Rosario, of about one million people."
Acindar has some 20 plants scattered over Argentina and one in Chile.
